item.title: We Finally Got Everything We Wanted—So Why Are We Fighting?
item.description:
Relationships

We Finally Got Everything We Wanted—So Why Are We Fighting?

Why achieving a long-term goal can create unexpected relationship tension.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Partners often have different expectations about what comes after success.
  • Accountability helps couples recognize how unspoken expectations contribute to conflict.
  • Repair strengthens relationships when values are recognized, respected, and integrated into a shared future.
Source: dotshock / 123rf.com

Julian and Theo had been together for seven years when they finally bought their first home. For much of their relationship, that goal shaped many of their decisions. While friends traveled, upgraded their lifestyles, or spent more freely, Julian and Theo focused on saving, planning, and building toward a future they both wanted.

Love: A Relationship Built Around a Shared Dream

The goal united them and gave them a shared sense of purpose. They spent evenings discussing neighborhoods, mortgage rates, and renovation ideas. Even when the sacrifices felt frustrating, they remained excited by the dream they were building together.

Julian, a project manager for a technology company, loved setting goals and creating plans. Theo, a high school art teacher, shared the dream but approached life differently. He valued enjoying the present as much as preparing for the future.

When they finally closed on the house, both felt proud. Years of discipline and teamwork had paid off. For a while, everything felt exactly as they had imagined. Then something unexpected happened. Without the goal of buying a home organizing their lives, they realized they were no longer moving in the same direction.

Crash: When Success Means Different Things

The first disagreements seemed minor. Julian immediately began thinking about what came next. There were rooms to repaint, projects to tackle, and financial goals to pursue. To him, the house marked the beginning of a new chapter. Theo experienced it differently. After years of postponing vacations and other pleasures, he wanted to enjoy what they had achieved. He imagined slower weekends, dinners with friends, and finally taking the trips they had postponed for years. Buying the house gave him permission to stop treating every decision as part of a larger financial strategy.

Instead of naturally resolving, the difference between them grew. Julian became frustrated when Theo showed little interest in future projects. Theo became discouraged that Julian kept talking about the next goal when they had barely celebrated the one they had just achieved. To Theo, every accomplishment seemed to generate another objective.

Conversations about spending, home improvements, and weekend plans gradually became more tense. The arguments themselves became less important than what they represented. No matter how often they talked, neither partner felt understood. Julian worried that Theo was becoming complacent and losing the drive they had always shared. Theo worried that Julian would never feel satisfied.

What neither recognized was that they held very different expectations about what life would look like after achieving their dream. For Julian, success created momentum; reaching one goal naturally led to another. For Theo, success created permission to pause, appreciate, and enjoy what they had worked so hard to build. Neither perspective was wrong. But because they never discussed those expectations openly, each gradually began experiencing the other as an obstacle rather than a partner.

In Love. Crash. Rebuild., we describe how rupture often develops when partners attach different meanings to the same experience. Julian experienced success as the beginning of the next challenge; Theo experienced it as permission to slow down and enjoy the life they had built together.

Rebuild: Using PACER to Navigate Success Together

Pause

The turning point came after an argument about a kitchen renovation spiraled into a much larger conversation. As they reflected on the disagreement, both realized they cared less about the renovation itself than they had claimed during the fight.

Pause helped them step back from the details and examine the deeper emotions underneath them. The issue was not the kitchen. It was that they had spent years preparing to achieve a goal and almost no time discussing what life would look like afterward. For the first time, they began talking openly about how differently they were experiencing this new chapter.

Accountability

Julian acknowledged that he often treated accomplishments as stepping stones rather than destinations. His focus on future goals sometimes prevented him from appreciating what they had already achieved together.

Theo acknowledged that he had quietly expected buying their home to bring a lasting sense of satisfaction. Rather than sharing those feelings, he withdrew because he did not want to disappoint or frustrate Julian. Neither partner intended to create distance. They simply entered this new stage of life with different expectations that they had never discussed.

Collaboration

As their conversations deepened, Julian and Theo began asking what they wanted this next chapter to represent. Julian realized that many of the projects he cared about were less about the house itself than about maintaining a sense of purpose and forward momentum. Theo realized that his desire to slow down was not a lack of ambition. He genuinely wanted time to appreciate the life they had worked so hard to create.

Instead of debating whose approach was right, they began asking a different question: How could they build a life that made room for both growth and enjoyment? That shift changed the conversation from competition to collaboration.

Experiment

They began making intentional adjustments. Some weekends remained dedicated to projects and planning. Others were intentionally protected from productivity.

They also created small rituals to celebrate accomplishments before immediately moving on to the next objective. Instead of treating milestones as brief stopping points, they practiced enjoying them together.

Most importantly, they began talking openly about success itself. What did "enough" actually look like? What kind of life were they trying to build? How could they protect their relationship while honoring that they sometimes wanted different things?

Reset

Over time, the emotional intensity surrounding these disagreements diminished. Julian felt less pressure to constantly create momentum. Theo felt less pressure to defend his desire to slow down and enjoy what they had accomplished. Their differences remained, but they no longer felt threatening.

The house continued to matter, yet it no longer carried the burden of defining their happiness. Instead, they developed a shared vision that balanced ambition with appreciation, future goals with present connection, and achievement with enjoyment.

Their relationship became stronger, not because they bought a house but because they learned how to navigate what came next.

Why This Matters

Many couples spend years preparing to achieve important goals but very little time discussing what happens after they reach them.

Whether the milestone is buying a home, getting married, finishing school, building a business, or reaching another long-sought dream, success often introduces a transition couples never anticipated. Once the goal has been achieved, differences in priorities, expectations, and definitions of fulfillment become more visible.

The PACER process helps couples slow down, explore the different meanings they attach to success, and create a shared vision for what comes next. Sometimes the challenge is not getting what you want. Sometimes the challenge is learning how to live together after you get it.

item.title: The Psychology of Flirting: What Actually Works
item.description:
Flirting

The Psychology of Flirting: What Actually Works

The most effective flirting strategy isn't the one most people expect.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • A person's decision about whether someone is attractive is made unconsciously.
  • The majority of the time, confidence, looks, or the right line aren't the most effective ways to flirt.
  • When people describe "chemistry," they often refer to their brain's ability to identify a connection.

Many people think that being successful at flirting depends on confidence, attractiveness, or a great pick-up line; however, research shows the truth is quite different.

Researchers evaluated nearly 1,000 participants (from both the USA and Norway) to determine which flirting methods yielded the most successful outcomes (Kennair et al., 2022).

The researchers were surprised to find that the most successful methods of flirting were not based on physical attractiveness, confidence, or the correct delivery of words. Instead, it has to do with how our minds work when evaluating the attractiveness of others.

Your Brain Makes Decisions Before You Do

When you first meet someone, the first moments of that meeting are more important than most people think.

Your brain starts asking a number of questions before you actually make the conscious decision of whether or not you like the person.

Will I be able to trust this person?

Will they understand me?

Will I be able to feel comfortable around them?

Will I enjoy spending more time with them?

Most of these processes happen automatically. During each moment in the interaction—whether it's a smile, gaze, or awkward pause—your brain is gathering data without you being aware of what it's doing.

Researchers have concluded that smiling and eye contact are major contributors to successful flirting (Kennair et al., 2022). These simple behaviors convey warmth and openness before you even have an actual conversation. Showing that your brain is not looking for perfection, only connection.

However, there was one flirting technique that was even higher-rated and had nothing to do with nonverbal behaviors.

What Scientists Found

A lot of people see flirting as an attempt to get someone excited or a way to get noticed. They do things to stand out, look good, and look perfect. But researchers have a different view of how successful flirting actually works.

According to a study conducted by researchers worldwide (Kennair et al., 2022), those who make the biggest impact on others are not those who try the hardest to show off; they're the ones who create a shared emotional experience with those they are attempting to flirt with.

This study involved thousands of respondents from both Norway and the United States. Researchers asked almost 1,000 people to evaluate a list of 40 different forms of flirting and rank them by which were best for both short-term and long-term relationships (Kennair et al., 2022).

The results from this large body of research showed that the best flirting was not being confident (in any form); dressing attractively (in any form); or creating a perfect opening line—instead, what researchers found was that the best way of flirting and buildng a bridge to another person was through humor followed by warm smiles, and eye contact (Kennair et al., 2022).

At first, given the simplicity of the answer, few people will believe this until they learn exactly what the act of laughing does within our brains.

The Neuroscience of Flirting

The power of humor is not in its entertainment value; it lies in its ability to forge connections between two people. When two individuals share a laugh, they are experiencing the same emotion in concert for a short period of time.

This phenomenon is referred to by psychologists as emotional synchrony, or the simultaneous response of two brains to an external stimulus. Ultimately, the chemistry between two individuals is shaped by this shared emotional experience.

In addition to creating connections, humor conveys social intelligence, emotional sensitivity, and an understanding of another's point of view. That’s why when one person laughs at another's jokes, they may very well be communicating what many words cannot: "I relate to you." Feeling understood is one of the most powerful ways people create a sense of connection.

Building Connection, Together

The ability to build a connection isn't something people either have or don’t have. The research in this study indicates that chemistry is not a magical stroke of good luck but rather the result of numerous small, individual interactions between two people: a smile, warm eye contact, feeling heard, and a good laugh.

While the individual moments of interaction that contribute to human connection do not guarantee that attraction will develop, they do create the right conditions for attraction to evolve.

This study primarily focused on the development of chemistry through flirting; however, it also demonstrated how people form strong human connections. The people we remember as being the most attractive, stylish, or self-assured are typically those who help us feel completely comfortable being ourselves.

Because, after all, the true purpose of flirting is to establish a connection between two people. Through flirting, we build a bridge to the other person that makes them feel safe enough to come over and connect.

Because the best flirting isn't really about impressing another person. It's about creating a connection that gives two brains a chance to decide: I like who I am when I’m with you.

item.title: Why the Most Dangerous Words Might Be Your Own
item.description:
Identity

Why the Most Dangerous Words Might Be Your Own

How identity, self-talk, and belief shape achievement.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Self-labels can become self-fulfilling prophecies that shape behaviour and performance.
  • The brain actively seeks evidence that confirms the identities we assign ourselves.
  • Success often creates psychological momentum that increases future achievement.
  • Positive self-talk and visualisation can strengthen confidence, motivation, and resilience.

Most people believe that success, happiness, and personal growth are primarily determined by intelligence, talent, opportunity, or hard work. While these factors undoubtedly matter, psychology suggests that something far more subtle may shape our lives every day: the labels we attach to ourselves.

Think about how often people describe themselves using fixed identities. Some say, "I am bad with money." Others insist, "I am not a confident person," "I am terrible at relationships," or "I am not leadership material." These statements often sound like simple observations. In reality, they may be acting as psychological instructions that influence future behaviour.

The labels we repeatedly assign to ourselves do not merely describe who we are. Over time, they can shape how we think, how we behave, and ultimately who we become. What begins as a passing thought can gradually develop into an identity, and identities are remarkably powerful forces in human behaviour.

How Identities Become Ingrained

The origins of this idea can be traced to labelling theory, which proposes that individuals often begin to behave in accordance with the labels assigned to them by society or by themselves (Becker, 1963). While the theory was initially developed to explain social behaviour, its implications extend far beyond sociology. In everyday life, people constantly create labels that influence their own self-concept. Once these labels become embedded within identity, they can affect decision-making, confidence, motivation, and performance.

The danger lies in the fact that the human mind seeks consistency. Once we adopt a particular identity, we unconsciously begin looking for evidence that supports it. A person who believes they are socially awkward might notice every uncomfortable interaction while overlooking successful conversations. Someone who believes they are unlucky could remember every setback while discounting moments of good fortune. This tendency is known as confirmation bias, whereby individuals seek information that reinforces their existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence (Nickerson, 1998).

As a result, labels often become self-fulfilling prophecies. Merton (1948) described how beliefs can influence behaviour in ways that ultimately make those beliefs appear true. A student who believes they are poor at mathematics may avoid studying, participate less in class, and approach examinations with anxiety. Unsurprisingly, their performance suffers. The poor result then appears to validate the original belief, even though the belief itself contributed to creating the outcome.

This phenomenon can be observed throughout life. Employees who believe they are capable are more likely to seek promotions, volunteer for challenging projects, and persevere when difficulties arise. Those who view themselves as inadequate may hesitate, withdraw, or avoid opportunities altogether. The difference is often not intelligence or talent but the expectations individuals hold about themselves.

Why "Winners Keep Winning": How Expectations Influence Action

One of the most fascinating examples of the power of expectations comes from Rosenthal and Jacobson's (1968) famous Pygmalion study. Teachers were informed that certain students were expected to show exceptional intellectual growth. Although these students had been randomly selected, they subsequently demonstrated greater academic improvement. The expectations of others subtly influenced behaviour, creating conditions that helped produce the anticipated outcome. If the expectations of others can shape our behaviour, it is reasonable to assume that our own expectations may have an even stronger influence.

This may help explain a phenomenon often described as "winners keep winning." Success rarely produces only external rewards. It also changes how individuals perceive themselves. Each achievement becomes evidence that they are capable, competent, and effective. These beliefs contribute to greater confidence, which encourages further action. As a result, success often generates psychological momentum.

Albert Bandura's (1977) concept of self-efficacy helps explain why some people continue to succeed despite challenges. Individuals who believe they can influence outcomes are more likely to persevere, recover from setbacks, and pursue opportunities. Over time, these behaviours increase the likelihood of success.

The opposite can also occur. Repeated failures or negative experiences may lead to learned helplessness, where people stop trying because they no longer believe their actions matter (Seligman, 1975). This can create a downward spiral, as individuals repeatedly label themselves as incapable or unsuccessful. Over time, these self-beliefs begin to shape their behaviour.

This is why positive self-talk matters. It is not about ignoring reality but about choosing language that encourages growth rather than limitation. Research suggests that constructive self-talk can improve motivation, performance, and resilience (Hatzigeorgiadis et al., 2011). Unfortunately, many people speak to themselves far more harshly than they would ever speak to a friend, gradually turning temporary setbacks into permanent identities.

The popular phrase "fake it till you make it" may contain more psychological truth than many realise. According to self-perception theory, people often develop beliefs about themselves by observing their own behaviour (Bem, 1972). In other words, acting confidently can help create confidence. When someone speaks up despite feeling nervous or pursues an opportunity despite self-doubt, they are not necessarily pretending; they are practising a future version of themselves.

A similar principle underlies visualisation. Research shows that mentally rehearsing an activity activates many of the same neural pathways involved in performing it (Driskell et al., 1994). Before a building is constructed, it exists as a blueprint; before a business is launched, it exists as an idea. Likewise, personal growth often begins with imagining a different version of oneself. Long before people become confident leaders, successful entrepreneurs, or accomplished professionals, they frequently envision that possibility.

This idea aligns with Carol Dweck's (2006) work on growth mindset. People who view their abilities as capable of development tend to achieve more than those who see their traits as fixed. The difference often lies in the labels they choose. Saying "I am bad at this" closes the door to growth, whereas saying "I am learning" keeps it open.

Ultimately, the labels we carry are rarely as permanent as we imagine. Many were formed years ago through criticism, failure, or difficult experiences, yet they continue to influence behaviour long after the original event has passed. The question is not simply who you are today, but who you repeatedly tell yourself you are. Your brain is always listening, and the identities you reinforce are often the identities you become.

item.title: Why You're Probably Not as Good a Listener as You Think
item.description:
Relationships

Why You're Probably Not as Good a Listener as You Think

While most people may mean well, research shows they don't listen well.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • While many people think they are good listeners, research shows that is not the case.
  • Many rush to give advice or reassurance, or they don't respond at all, which can feel dismissive.
  • The good thing is that listening is a skill that can be improved and refined with practice.
Source: Image by Stephan Sigg from Pixabay

Most of us like to believe we're good listeners.

We tell our friends, "I'm here if you need me." We encourage loved ones to reach out when they're struggling. We think of ourselves as supportive, compassionate people. But when someone actually comes to us with their pain, many of us don't know what to do.

Most of us think we are better at listening than we are

The friend who says, "You can talk to me anytime," but never responds to your texts when you do reach out. The listener who turns the conversation back to their own experiences before you've even finished telling your story.

The person who becomes so uncomfortable with your pain that they rush to reassure you that everything will be okay: "You'll figure it out!" Even well-intended responses, "I'll pray for you," can sometimes feel dismissive if they aren't accompanied by presence and support.

Most of us have probably been on both sides of these interactions. If you're thinking, "I'm a pretty good listener," you're not alone. Most of us believe we're better at listening than we actually are. People tend to overestimate their interpersonal skills, including their ability to understand and respond to others effectively.1,2 At the same time, our minds frequently wander during conversations, and many of us spend more time preparing our response than truly listening to the person speaking.2 Rather than focusing on understanding, we often focus on solving, reassuring, comparing, or figuring out the "right" thing to say.

Like many human skills, listening suffers from a common problem: most of us think we're better at it than we are.

Caring and listening aren't always the same thing

People feel most heard when listeners demonstrate curiosity, ask thoughtful follow-up questions, reflect understanding, and remain present without rushing to offer advice or solutions. Unfortunately, many of us do the opposite. We interrupt with our own stories, jump into problem-solving mode, or reassure people before fully understanding what they're trying to say. The result isn't necessarily that we're uncaring—it’s that listening is a far more active and challenging skill than most of us realize.

The problem is that many of us were never taught what listening actually looks like. We learned how to talk, persuade, explain, and problem-solve. We learned how to make conversation. But few of us learned how to sit with another person's pain without trying to fix it. When someone shares a struggle, discomfort often takes over, and many of us scramble away. We feel pressure to make them feel better. We search for advice, silver linings, or solutions, often because these things make us feel better; we assume they will make the other person feel better, too. In doing so, we sometimes stop listening altogether.

The truth is that most of us are probably worse listeners than we think. The good news is that listening is a skill: it can be learned, practiced, and strengthened.

Here are a couple of quick tips:

  1. Reflect before you respond.
    Instead of jumping into advice or your own story, briefly mirror what you heard: “That sounds really overwhelming,” as this signals understanding before anything else. After they have had their chance to share, you can make the connection to your own story.
  2. Ask one real follow-up question.
    Even asking just one curious question opens the door a little wider: “What was that like for you to hear that?” or “What happened next?” Questions signal that you are interested, which makes the person feel listened to.

item.title: Hybrid FOMO: Why Are We So Afraid to Be Left Behind Amid AI?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Hybrid FOMO: Why Are We So Afraid to Be Left Behind Amid AI?

Four steps to preserve your mind in the midst of AI, from the inside out.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Hybrid FOMO is fear of missing out on the emerging partnership between natural and artificial intelligences.
  • People fear AI because it may make their skills less valuable.
  • People also fear avoiding AI because avoidance may make their skills obsolete.

A strange new anxiety has sat down with us in meeting rooms and online forums; it hovers over group chats and appears whenever someone says, “I am using AI for this.” Or “AI has made me so much more productive at that.” These sentences are often casual; their effect is not.

One person finishes a report in half the time. Another builds a presentation overnight. A student produces a polished essay before dinner. A colleague speaks in prompts, agents, copilots, and workflows. Suddenly, the mind begins its private arithmetic: What do they know that I don’t? What are they becoming that I am not? Am I (too) late?

The Rise of Hybrid FOMO

This is hybrid FOMO: the fear of missing out on the emerging partnership between natural and artificial intelligences. Old FOMO was social: Other people were at the party, on the trip, in the photo. Hybrid FOMO is existential. Other people seem to be upgrading their minds, whereas we are bound to be left behind.

Hybrid FOMO: the fear of missing out on the emerging partnership between natural and artificial intelligences. Old FOMO was social: other people were at the party, on the trip, in the photo. Hybrid FOMO is existential. Other people seem to be upgrading their minds whereas we are bound to be left behind.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

Intuitively, FOMO makes sense. As humans, we are exquisitely tuned to status, belonging, and competence. The original psychological research on fear of missing out linked it to unmet needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. When we feel less capable, less connected, or less in control, we become more vulnerable to the sense that life is happening elsewhere. A recent three-wave longitudinal study on FOMO and social media described it as a kind of “self-regulatory limbo”: We check because we feel unsettled, then checking over and again keeps the unsettled feeling alive.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adds further fuel because it changes the meaning of “elsewhere.” Elsewhere is no longer Ibiza, Davos, or the dinner we missed. Elsewhere is the future of work, arriving in someone else’s browser tab.

The numbers explain part of the unease. In 2025, a Pew Research Center survey found that 52 percent of U.S. workers felt worried about future AI use in the workplace, while only 36 percent felt hopeful. About a third felt overwhelmed. The emotional cocktail is telling: worry, hope, overwhelm, excitement. Hybrid FOMO rarely comes as pure fear. It arrives as a racing blend of curiosity and threat. Another part is speed.

The Role of Speed

The Stanford 2025 AI Index notes that AI capability, adoption, investment, and regulation are all moving at unusual velocity. The cost of using models has fallen sharply. Smaller models have become more capable. Businesses report far more AI use than only a year earlier. For the ordinary mind, this creates temporal vertigo. We are trying to make calm decisions inside an accelerating narrative.

Yet the most interesting question is psychological: Why does AI make so many people feel personally behind?

Because AI does three things at once.

  • First, it makes invisible effort visible. Before generative AI, a skilled colleague’s advantage could be explained by experience, talent, training, or time. Now the output appears without the labor trail. A polished memo, a beautiful image, a coded prototype, a market scan, a grant draft: All can materialize with suspicious speed. The observer sees the result, guesses at the tool, and feels a private loss of rank. Hybrid FOMO grows in the gap between visible output and invisible process.
  • Second, AI threatens competence while offering the pretense of competence. This is the paradox. People fear AI because it may make their skills less valuable. They also fear avoiding AI because avoidance may make their skills obsolete. Use it, and one may feel dependent. Ignore it, and one may feel outdated. A Springer review on AI anxiety describes apprehension linked to the rapid advance of AI technologies. The anxiety is sharpened by ambiguity: People do not know which tasks will be transformed, which skills will rise, which skills will fade, and how quickly the sorting will happen.
  • Third, AI alters the social imagination. We compare ourselves less with who others are and more with what others can now produce. Social comparison becomes productive comparison. The question changes from “Do they have a better life?” to “Do they have a better mind-machine combination?”

Freedom From Hybrid FOMO, Inside Out

Hybrid FOMO is partly a fear of exclusion from a new form of cognition. Individuals sense, often correctly, that the next advantage belongs neither to humans alone nor to machines alone. It belongs to those who learn how to combine judgment, taste, ethics, memory, curiosity, and machine speed. Hybrid intelligence is becoming a social signal.

Research already shows why the signal is confusing. In the “jagged technological frontier” study, 758 consultants using GPT-4 improved on many tasks: They completed more work, moved faster, and produced higher-quality results. On a task outside AI’s capability frontier, the AI-assisted group performed worse. This is the trap. AI can make a person look brilliantly augmented in one situation and confidently wrong in another. Hybrid FOMO pushes people to use the tool everywhere. Hybrid wisdom asks where the tool belongs, harnessing hybrid intelligence to orchestrate a wide range of assets deliberately. That choice requires insight and confidence in one’s own skills.

A 2025 Microsoft Research study on generative AI and critical thinking found that higher confidence in AI was associated with less critical thinking, while higher self-confidence was associated with more critical thinking. That result is a small key for a large lock. The safest AI users may be those who trust themselves enough to challenge the machine.

Hybrid FOMO, therefore, points to a deeper need: agency. We do not merely want access to the newest tool. We want assurance that we can still steer our lives with dignity. The fear of being left behind is also the fear of becoming mentally passive in a world that rewards acceleration.

The cure is less dramatic than the anxiety. No one needs to master every model, chase every update, or become fluent in every platform. The wiser move is to build a personal rhythm of hybrid competence.

Use AI where it expands your reach. Pause where it weakens your attention. Learn in public enough to belong. Practice in private enough to retain your own mind.

The FOMO Takeaway

F — Find your frontier. Choose four recurring tasks: one where AI can save time, one where it can improve quality, and two where human judgment must lead. Experiment deliberately.

O — Own your baseline. Before using AI, write your own first paragraph, sketch your own idea, or define your own question. Give the machine something human to work with.

M — Make learning social. Create a small AI learning circle with colleagues or friends. Share prompts, failures, surprises, and ethical worries. FOMO shrinks when learning becomes shared.

O — Opt for agency. Decide what you will delegate, what you will co-create, and what you will keep human. The goal is not to keep up with every tool. The goal is to remain the author of your attention, your judgment, and your becoming.

item.title: Meditation: The Mental Edge You Didn't Know You Needed
item.description:
Meditation

Meditation: The Mental Edge You Didn't Know You Needed

Beyond stress relief, research shows meditation sharpens cognition and more.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Meditation sharpens cognitive skills, aiding learning and focus beyond just stress reduction.
  • Mindfulness meditation can perceptually slow time, helping rapid decision-making under pressure.
  • Neurologic changes from meditation enhance areas tied to memory, awareness, and emotion regulation.
Source: Lisa Runnels / Pixabay

Meditation is a mental training skill, successfully used regularly by high performers such as elite athletes, those in high-risk occupations, and corporate executives. Much of the meditation literature focuses on stress reduction and physical and mental health; however, meditation is so much more. Our highest performers have discovered that we can use it to hone our skills, learn more effectively, and improve our attentional and other cognitive abilities.

This is not to say that it isn’t an important component of complementary medicine (i.e., techniques used to complement traditional medical interventions). Meditation can augment treatment for both medical and mental health conditions by lowering stress reactivity, improving emotional regulation and mood, decreasing blood pressure, and helping to manage pain and chronic medical conditions. But more to the point of this post, for literally thousands of years, people have practiced meditation because it provides daily benefits that can make us more effective versions of ourselves.

The power of meditation as mental training

As noted above, it is a mental training skill based on techniques that focus or clear your mind, while it also involves nonjudgmental awareness and acceptance.

While many of us think of meditation as an activity done sitting on the floor in the lotus position, there is a wide variety of styles and techniques. You can meditate while sitting in a chair or in a comfortable position on the floor. Those with back pain or other concerns can also lie down, although the risk is that you fall asleep. Techniques can include deep breathing, mindfulness, mantras, and even walking.

Meditation is a powerful tool, and given its substantial potential benefits and limited risks, it is well worth exploring. Consider the following:

  • Meditation is accessible to all. One of the great characteristics of meditation is that it is free and available to everyone; you don’t need to be in good physical shape to do it; and you don’t need to leave your house. You can buy equipment with which to meditate; however, this isn’t necessary. Additionally, a simple internet search of “guided meditation” will give you more free videos than you could ever need if you’d like someone to take you through a guided meditation session. Try a few, and find a style you like.
  • Meditation alters time perception. One study looked at time perception in the context of meditation and found that subjects who engaged in mindfulness meditation were more likely to overestimate time compared to a control group. This finding that meditation perceptually slows time makes it extremely valuable for those in high-stress or high-risk occupations who need to make rapid, high-stakes decisions. Sometimes you need to slow down to speed up.
  • Meditation improves cognition and changes your brain. A number of studies have found neurologic differences between those who meditate and those who do not, particularly in areas of the brain involved in memory, awareness, and emotional regulation. Also, studies looking at the effect of meditation on cognitive abilities have found substantial benefits to meditating in the areas of working memory, reading comprehension, and attention. Even short, one-time meditation sessions improve cognition and performance. For example, college students who meditated before exams performed better than their peers who did not, and medical students who engaged in a short, focused meditation session improved their working memory of number strings.

Human performance, wellness, and holistic medicine programs are tapping into what some cultures have known for thousands of years. Meditation is a powerful tool, not just for health and well-being, but for performance, achievement, and self-efficacy. It is a practical mental skill that can strengthen attention, emotional regulation, learning, memory, and performance under pressure. Whether you want to focus on your mental or physical health, excel professionally, or simply become a more focused and resilient version of yourself, meditation offers a highly accessible, evidence-based way to do so.

item.title: A New Clue Linking Depression to the Immune System
item.description:
Depression

A New Clue Linking Depression to the Immune System

A new mind-body connection hidden in our immune cells.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • The brain and body interact more closely than traditionally believed.
  • Physical Inflammatory illnesses can profoundly influence mental health outcomes.
  • Aging of immune cells correlate with emotional depressive symptoms, not physical.
  • Findings strengthen mind-body links while raising enduring philosophical questions again.

For hundreds of years, the central nervous system and the body have been assumed to be two distinct territories. The brain was regarded as the center of consciousness, thoughts, emotions, and decisions, and the body was seen as the executor of the brain's commands and the receiver of sensory information. The discovery of the blood-brain barrier by German physician Paul Ehrlich in the 19th century reinforced this belief. This barrier protects the brain from potentially harmful blood-derived compounds. However, to allow the entry of essential substances, such as amino acids and glucose, into the neural tissues of the central nervous system, the barrier contains several specific transport systems.

Even physicians who specialize in either the brain or the body believe that medical conditions affecting these two distinct areas have different roots. The field of psychological and mental diseases was considered totally different from physical pathology. This was, at least in part, due to the unwanted historical influence of old scholars who believed that the brain is the seat of the sacred soul or mind. In this brain-centric view, mental states are solely brain functions, with body conditions influenced by separate factors.

The Brain-Body Connection

However, recent findings in both mental and physical disorders reveal that these two apparently distinct entities interact with each other. Growing evidence shows that inflammation—metabolic diseases, cancer, arthritis, and cardiovascular diseases—can affect the nervous system through various mechanisms. Neuroinflammation originating in the body impairs brain function and may lead to mental disorders, including anxiety and depression, and is even associated with Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Conversely, mental disorders have been shown to contribute to several physical pathologies, such as heart disease, diabetes, and immune system disorders.[1]

Another notable example of a physical illness primarily affecting the brain is liver dysfunction, whether genetic or acquired, which leads to increased ammonia levels. This ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and harms the brain.

Conversely, the regulatory brain's role in almost everything we do—controlling bodily systems and organs, and maintaining internal stability, or homeostasis—is especially important. The immune system is crucial for fighting pathogens, cancer cells, and damaged cells, and is controlled by the brain through neuroendocrine mechanisms. Mental states have a potent impact on normal responses and stopping inflammation. It is well recognized that stress and anxiety decline immune function and prolong inflammation.

As mentioned above, depression is often thought of as a condition of the mind, but growing evidence suggests it may also leave traces in the body. Now, a recent study published in The Journals of Gerontology adds a new layer to this emerging picture by examining not inflammation itself, but the biological age of immune cells. Researchers measured the "epigenetic age" of monocytes (a type of white blood cell) in 440 women, about 60 percent of whom were living with HIV. Researchers found that women whose immune cells showed signs of premature aging were more likely to have experienced emotional symptoms of depression, like losing interest in things, feeling unmotivated, or hopeless. Surprisingly, these same cells do not link to physical symptoms such as tiredness or changes in appetite. The premature aging of immune cells was associated only with the mental and emotional side of depression, leaving its bodily manifestations untouched. The study does not claim causation; it only shows a correlation. But the very existence of this selective connection, between a cellular event and a subjective feeling, is what makes it so provocative.[2]

They do not claim to have found a diagnostic tool. Instead, this study highlights a possibility: Some emotional symptoms of depression may be reflected in the biology of the immune system. Although the idea of analyzing mental disorders through blood tests has been proposed before, future research may reveal whether measuring the biological age of immune cells via a blood test may help identify people at risk for depression or guide more personalized treatments.[3]

The Dialogue Between Mind and Body

What they do offer is a clearer picture of the bidirectional dialogue between mind and body. With today's knowledge, perhaps Descartes, Leibniz, Hume, and Locke would have rethought dualism. We now know that mental states shape physical states, and bodily systems shape mental states.

However, these findings also revive questions that have long occupied philosophers of mind. If the mind is nothing but identical to brain processes, why does a physical change in immune cells align so specifically with a subjective experience, a loss of pleasure, a collapse of meaning? The materialist might answer that brain functions regulate both immunity and consciousness in parallel. But that answer does not solve the mystery; it simply shifts it elsewhere. Even if mind and immunity are twin effects of a common neural cause, the experience of hopelessness remains irreducibly first-person, untranslatable into cell counts or biological clock speeds.

The old dualists were right that the mind feels real. The materialists are right that the mind is embodied. But both are wrong to think the problem is simple. Perhaps this study does not solve the mind-body puzzle; it simply shows us a new place to look for it, in the strange space where a cell's age meets a feeling of despair, and where science must finally bow to philosophy.

item.title: A Lesson From Getting Pantsed
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

A Lesson From Getting Pantsed

Personal Perspective: An act of disrespect shows the power of setting boundaries.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Teaching kids to set boundaries empowers them to protect both physical and emotional space.
  • Many families avoid teaching relational boundaries, leaving kids unprepared for self-advocacy.
  • Suppressing needs often leads to resentment, passive-aggression, and codependency in adulthood.
Source: Photo by Tanya Prodaan on Unsplash

During recess on the last week of school, our 10-year-old son got pantsed by a couple of kids. He was rightfully upset and chased them down. Fortunately, he did not resort to violence, but he made it very clear that they were never to touch him again or he would defend himself in the future.

The incident was reported to staff, and the principal intervened and spoke with the boys responsible. Apparently, they had been doing it to several other kids on the playground as well. Some children felt humiliated and were seen crying. Others turned inward and stayed silent. I have always insisted that our son express his feelings, so he never has to keep things bottled up or wonder whether anyone cares about his concerns.

I am proud that our son has learned early in life that he has a right to demand that his physical boundaries be respected. More importantly, he understands that he also has a right to express emotional boundaries. He knows the power of the word no, and he is willing to use it. Watching him stand up for himself made me reflect that I did not learn this right until much later in my adult life.

The Importance of Teaching Relational Boundaries in Families

In therapy, one of the biggest lessons I see missing from many families is the teaching of relational boundaries. Whether because of culture, religion, or family dynamics, many parents are hesitant to teach their children how to establish and maintain healthy boundaries. Relational boundaries mean helping children understand that they have a right to express their needs, preferences, thoughts, and feelings. That does not mean parents kowtow to their kids, but it does mean children are allowed to have a voice.

In many traditional Asian households, that right can quickly become viewed as wrong. Children learn that their parents do not see them as independent people with their own autonomy and self-expression. Instead, they are taught to obey, conform, and avoid disagreement. Some of this stems from centuries-old Confucian and cultural values that emphasize collectivism, harmony, and group cohesion. While those values have strengths, they can also create real challenges later in life when adults struggle to identify their own needs, wants, and emotions.

As a child, I learned this way of relating. Stay quiet, stuff it down, let others mistreat you. So that is exactly what happened. In elementary school, I allowed a classmate to repeatedly slap me on the back of the neck at school. I never said a word. I simply let it happen.

As an adult, I would later endure racial slurs and insults directed at me in public. I let those slide, too. I vividly remember one incident at a bar when my girlfriend at the time was targeted as well. She turned to me and said, “Aren’t you going to say anything?!” I shrugged my shoulders and pretended it didn’t bother me. Inside, I was seething. I felt violated and angry about the injustice, but I also felt powerless to speak up or even report it to management.

Even in less offensive situations, I struggled to express what I wanted. During college, I worked at Red Robin with the goal of becoming a waiter. I watched the girls who had been hired up to a year after me quickly go from hosting to server, while I remained a busser. I assumed hard work alone would eventually earn me a promotion. That’s what my parents told me growing up. “Don’t say anything. Do good work. Your bosses will reward you. Just keep quiet.” That’s the Asian way, but it’s not the American way.

A coworker gave me a reality check. He said, “Sam, if you want to be a waiter, you have to demand it!” He pointed to Roger, a guy who had been a busser for four years. “If you don’t say anything, you’re going to be like him!” It was so countercultural to hear this. What about the dedication and loyalty I had already shown? Looking back, it was one of my earliest lessons in self-advocacy.

It does not get easier in dating and marriage. When you consistently suppress your needs and desires, even when you know they may not be met, resentment, passive-aggressive behavior, and codependency can begin to take root. I know because that was me. I became known as a “yes” man.

During my first marriage, which ended more than 25 years ago, I simply went along with whatever my ex wanted. She wanted me to drop my Chinese surname and adopt her Korean last name, so I did. She wanted to move by herself from Ohio to New York so she could pursue an acting career, while I stayed in Ohio. I agreed. When concerned friends questioned the decision, I responded with generic platitudes like, “Love is about sacrifice!”

In my first career in television broadcasting, I also failed to establish physical boundaries. I allowed a manager to make unwanted sexual advances toward me without reporting it. I felt obligated to comply, even drinking more alcohol than I wanted to. Eventually, the situation escalated beyond what I was comfortable with before I finally said stop.

A close relative later asked me, “Why didn’t you just say no?!” I responded, “Because I didn’t think I could.” He looked at me, perplexed.

That is why, when I hear stories involving poor boundaries in therapy or life, I understand. I never ask why someone couldn’t say anything against domestic violence, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, verbal abuse, or racial abuse. Often, the ability to establish boundaries was never taught in the first place. And what is not taught can easily be passed down to the next generation unless we consciously choose to teach something different.

The Value of Learning to Say No

Looking back, I am grateful that our son already knows something that took me decades to learn: the right to say no. He has the right to speak up when he feels disrespected. He has the right to protect his boundaries.

Maybe that’s the real lesson from getting pantsed on a playground. It’s not about the pants. It’s about dignity and the ability to stand up for your own self-worth.

item.title: The Dark Side of Work Cultures
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

The Dark Side of Work Cultures

Co-workers who appear "nice" may be hiding something darker.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Cultures that look nice on the surface may enforce silence and quiet employee voice.
  • Normative niceness, the pressure to be agreeable and non-confrontational, suppresses authentic conversation.
  • Sustainability initiatives were ignored when employees felt unsafe to question leaders' decisions.

Written by Clare Burns, Ph.D., and Melissa Wheeler, Ph.D.

Wouldn’t it be wonderful to work with good colleagues? For many, an ideal work environment is one where people are kind to each other, they make supportive comments, bring cupcakes to mark special occasions, and celebrate each other’s wins. But what if these nice acts are camouflaging something more sinister?

Source: Karola / Pexels

Recent research by Bond University’s Clare Burns (and one of the authors of this post) introduced a paradox lurking behind nice work cultures.

Modern workplaces that pride themselves on being nice can simultaneously sustain rigid hierarchies—speaking up feels risky and questioning authority is quietly but firmly discouraged. Entrenched hierarchies create cultures of high power distances, where there are big gaps between leaders and subordinates.

This paradox results in a culture that looks friendly on the surface but tacitly enforces silence and quiets employee voice.

Niceness as a Defensive Strategy

Many organizations proudly espouse egalitarian values, claiming all workers are valued and can speak up. Indeed, some have the words “courageous,” “brave,” and “collaborative” displayed in their meeting rooms. These words project virtue but often bear little resemblance to the day-to-day assumptions of the people who work in the organization.

This curated appearance looks good from the outside, but insiders experience a different reality. Normative niceness, or the pressure to be agreeable and non-confrontational, acts like a control mechanism. In such environments, challenging the status quo is often perceived as incivility, causing people to keep their opinions to themselves. This suppression hurts people, organizations, and their stakeholders.

In this new research, managers of a large financial organization admitted they had not fully grasped the depth of the normative niceness expectations. They described being sent to coaching to moderate their direct, and supposedly “not nice,” communication styles. Frontline staff are aware that it is not nice to speak up; one shared that they had witnessed their colleagues speak up, only to face informal excommunication, leaving departure from the organization as their only option.

The study revealed that in-house staff surveys showed that employees felt comfortable raising challenging issues, but this was likely untrue. When external research was conducted, employees changed their story, reflecting that they were “dead scared” of saying or doing the wrong thing.

Authentic conversations were not happening, as being nice meant staying quiet. In such high-power-distance cultures, niceness was used as a systematized tool to protect directors from an uncomfortable confrontation.

Smiling Through Silence and the Impact on Sustainability

When employees learn that speaking up is not an acceptable norm, they figure out it is better to smile and nod at a superior’s comments.

Normative niceness may be subtle but can be highly effective in shaping culture. Can creativity thrive in normatively nice cultures? Surrounded by performative niceness, employees do not feel safe to offer suggestions that fall outside their managers’ comfort zones, nor do they feel comfortable articulating risks. A systematic voice–silence loop is created that does not reward speaking up or initiating tough conversations.

Within this command-and-control culture, espoused commitments to sustainability were not actualized. Sustainability goals were only talk, because financial logic, based on short-term profit, was the dominant model. Sustainability initiatives suffered when employees felt unsafe to question heavy investment in fossil-fuel-producing assets or the disconnect between what was written in corporate sustainability reports and the day-to-day reality.

Within the study, some participants stated there was a dark side to cultures that enforced agreeableness. Employees were aware that if they questioned topics such as greenwashing, they would be ostracized. Therefore, they stayed quiet, and their organization continued to neglect sustainability.

How Can Organizations Support Sustainability?

Resolving this niceness-sustainability paradox takes moral courage from directors. This means they need to be ready to receive uncomfortable feedback from employees and other stakeholders. It requires breaking long-standing defensive mechanisms, which include creating a psychologically safe climate where:

  • The director's role model is constructive dissent
  • There is an open dialogue about where the organization is failing in its decision-making processes
  • Everyday practices and structures are implemented so that environmental and social considerations are heard alongside economic ones.
  • Staff are incentivized to speak up on sustainability issues and opportunities as part of their remuneration package.

Nice behavior, where people smile and agree even though they know what is being said is untrue, does not create cultures of kindness. These cultures are not good for employees or the organization in the long run. But change is possible if the tone is set and remodeled from the top, making difficult conversations a part of everyday work.

Co-author Clare Burns is an assistant professor at Bond University in Australia.

item.title: Are We Really Living in a Simulation?
item.description:
Cognition

Are We Really Living in a Simulation?

Critically thinking about expertise and the nature of existence.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Some believe that the universe is actually a simulation.
  • Just because something is a possibility doesn’t make it the case.
  • We can use critical thinking to consider expert perspectives before accepting a new idea as true.

As I mention often on this blog, I have a great interest in the universe—astrophysics, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all that stuff. With that, I’m no expert in any of it. I just enjoy reading and watching videos about it. Recently, I’ve found myself being fed the same headlines over and over again—that the universe is actually a simulation—an idea that’s been around a while, but really seems to be getting a push in my algorithm. I’ve even seen a few pieces argue for the increased likelihood that we live in a simulation in light of how many "scientists"/"experts" now believe it themselves. As I also often argue here, if most experts agree on something, then we should probably give them the benefit of the doubt when we’re not experts in that field. However, as critical thinkers, it is still up to us to confirm the credibility of this expertise and determine whether the experts actually do agree and believe it themselves, and so, that’s what I did here.

Background on the Simulation Argument

To begin, a little background—the simulation argument first started to take off in the early 2000s, when philosopher Nick Bostrom made the point that if a civilisation were to develop to the point where it could create a conscious simulation, it could generate them over and over. The "first" reality, or base reality, might create a second, and the second eventually create a third, and the third eventually a fourth, and so on (like a Russian nesting doll scenario). Thus, from a potentially infinite series of simulations, if you were to randomly select a single "individual," statistically speaking, it’s most likely that they were a part of a simulated reality, as opposed to the base reality.

Of course, consistent with a previous post, in which I mentioned that we as a society have a significant problem in terms of our familiarity with academics or their research, I imagine not many people have heard of Nick Bostrom. However, as part of pop culture, most people do know Elon Musk, who publicly shared his belief in the simulation argument about a decade ago and has since elaborated upon it a variety of times. Sure, Elon is a smart guy, but he’s not an expert in this field. Some might argue that Bostrom isn’t either.

In terms of understanding the universe and cosmology, the three experts that immediately pop into my head are also somewhat famous in the sense that anyone who has ever watched a credible documentary on these types of topics would be familiar with their work: Brian Cox, Neil deGrasse Tyson, and Michio Kaku. Their takes on the simulation argument are interesting.

Cox addresses it as a philosophical idea, rather than a testable hypothesis, and is thus sceptical of the concept in light of zero evidence to suggest simulation as a valid theory. DeGrasse Tyson entertains the idea in a diplomatic manner by saying, on his podcast "StatTalk," that it’s more a 50/50 case than a statistical likelihood that we live in a simulation because of a number of ignored assumptions (i.e., Bostrom’s initial argument addresses that we might not live in a simulation, but if we ever have the capability and choose to engage it, then we likely are; see also David Kipping’s take on the argument)—primarily the case that it would require living in a reality where such simulation can be conducted. As we don’t have the capability to conduct such a simulation yet, we are either in the base reality where it hasn’t happened yet (i.e., not a simulation), or we are in the most recent iteration of simulation (regardless of being the second, fifth, or 1 trillion-and-ninth), where it also hasn’t happened yet; thus, 50/50. Kaku, on the other hand, like Cox, is highly sceptical. Kaku calls it speculative and argues the impossibility of such a concept, as the processing required would exceed the limitations of any machine existing within that reality. Kaku’s perspective is also supported by a body of research suggesting the same. So, all in all, it doesn’t seem very likely, from the perspective of the experts addressed here, that we’re living in a simulation.

Psychological Implications of the Simulation Argument

So, what? What’s this got to do with psychology? The answer is two-fold. First, some people find such reports to be alarming and scary. What if we really were living in a simulation? What would that mean for you as a person? What would it mean for your family? How do such thoughts make you feel? Does it create existential dread or cause you stress? If so, hopefully this endeavour into expert opinion has made you feel better about things. Don’t let fear or emotion override good thinking. The simulation argument simply represents a philosophical take on existence, with arguably as much strength as an absurdist approach (as discussed previously on this blog) or any other philosophical perspective might have. Sure, some experts do entertain it as "possible," but just because something is a possibility doesn’t make it the case. So, I wouldn’t worry too much about it! If such discussion doesn’t elicit any stress, great! Then consider the second point: hopefully, this piece has represented a good example of reinforcing this blog’s ongoing message about expertise and credibility.

My handle on Twitter is @CogitoErgoDwyer, a play on Descartes’ Cogito Ergo Sum—"I think, therefore I am." Indeed, we’ve dealt with this existential dilemma for centuries. The concept is not new. We exist—at least, that’s what the experts seem to suggest, as discussed above. Likewise, the handle reflects my area of research—this is a blog about human cognition, about thinking. Specifically, it is a blog about critical thinking, so let’s think critically… from what source are you getting your information? When it comes to the nature of the universe, I’m not listening to pseudo-intellectual businessmen with a BSc; I want to hear it from the experts. Despite finding them so entertaining to read, as a sci-fi fan, I certainly don’t want to hear about how an example of a "glitch in the matrix" represents evidence—that’s not evidence; that’s an anecdote marred by your bias. Again, understanding credibility is important.

My algorithm keeps feeding me sensationalist reports pertaining to cosmology, the universe, and philosophy because they reflect my interests. But the algorithm doesn’t decipher the credibility for me; that’s something I have to do myself, and likewise, what you have to do for yourselves. Thus, this piece isn’t just about the simulation argument; it’s also about using critical thinking to potentially put your mind at ease and/or (at the very least) a further example of the importance of obtaining expert perspectives before accepting a new idea as true.

item.title: 7 Signs You're in Bed With an Avoidant Partner
item.description:
Attachment

7 Signs You're in Bed With an Avoidant Partner

How avoidant attachment style impacts intimacy, desire, and your sex life.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Avoidant attachment often allows for physical closeness while keeping emotional intimacy at arm's length.
  • From rushing through foreplay to avoiding cuddles, they can leave their partners feeling abandoned.
  • Lasting relationships require a willingness to heal, communicate, and move toward secure connection.
Source: Lopolo / Shutterstock

They are the lone wolves of the attachment world. Independent, self-sufficient, and often effortlessly charming, avoidant individuals can seem like they have it all together. But underneath all that confidence lies a deep discomfort with meaningful connections.

Avoidant attachment often develops in homes where emotions are ignored, dismissed, criticized, or even punished. Parents may struggle to express their own feelings or become uncomfortable when their children express theirs. When children are shamed for crying, humiliated for expressing fear, or scolded for being "too sensitive," they begin to experience their emotions as threats. To protect themselves, they shut down their emotional needs and learn to face the world alone (Balan, 2023).

As adults, these individuals often appear confident, successful, capable, composed, and low-maintenance. They may enjoy relationships, sex, and companionship, but true emotional intimacy is almost always off the table. The closer someone gets, the stronger the urge to retreat (Johnson, 2019).

In many cases, these defenses follow couples into the bedroom. Here are seven signs you may be sleeping with an avoidant partner.

1. They'll Sleep With You But Won't Reveal Themselves

Your partner may be comfortable with physical closeness but become noticeably uncomfortable when conversations turn vulnerable. They can share a bed with you but struggle to share their fears, insecurities, or deeper emotions. While sex may feel natural, being truly known can feel extremely intimidating.

You may find yourself knowing their cover stories but feeling disconnected from who they really are. Even in long-term relationships, you may sense that there is a wall between you. They reveal enough to maintain the relationship but rarely allow themselves to be fully seen.

2. Foreplay Feels Like a Chore

Your partner may rush through foreplay and treat it as something to get over with. Foreplay often requires slowing down, tuning into another person's needs, and building anticipation. For an avoidant partner, prolonged eye contact, affectionate touch, and emotional presence can feel uncomfortable or even threatening (Schachner & Shaver, 2004). For someone who learned early in life to keep vulnerability at arm's length, the closeness that foreplay invites can feel difficult to tolerate. Sex may feel more physical than intimate, leaving you with the unsettling feeling that you're sharing a bed with someone who is miles away.

3. No Cuddles, No Pillow Talk

You may notice a pattern where your partner becomes distant after sex. They may roll over, reach for their phone, or trot to the kitchen to make popcorn. If you spend the night together, they may leave before you wake up or call you an Uber.

Cuddling, pillow talk, and quiet moments of connection can feel too intimate for an avoidant partner. Once sex is over, their defenses often return. Even small gestures of meaningful connection can make them uncomfortable, causing them to pull away just when you are hoping to get closer (Balan, 2024).

4. Every Serious Conversation Hits a Wall

When conversations about sexual needs, desires, insecurities, or connection arise, your partner may suddenly become uncomfortable. They might crack a joke, change the subject, become distracted by their phone, or retreat altogether.

Many avoidant individuals struggle with conversations that require openness and self-disclosure. Discussing fears, unmet needs, disappointments, or relationship concerns can leave them feeling trapped, criticized, or overwhelmed. Rather than lean into the conversation, they often look for the nearest exit.

Over time, you may find yourself talking around important issues rather than through them. Physical intimacy may exist, but meaningful conversations rarely get very far.

5. They Keep Intimacy on Their Terms

Avoidant individuals often feel most comfortable when they are in control of the timing, pace, and intensity of intimacy. They may initiate sex when they desire contact but become distant when you seek reassurance or affection. Intimacy can begin to feel one-sided, leaving you unsure when they will lean in and when they will pull away.

The unpredictability can be confusing. One day, they may seem warm, engaged, and affectionate; the next, they may appear distant and unavailable. This push-pull dynamic can leave partners confused about the right balance of getting close and giving space.

6. They Prefer Fantasy to Vulnerability

Some avoidant individuals feel more comfortable engaging with fantasy, pornography, or detached sexual experiences than with the unpredictability of a real relationship.

Contrary to popular belief, avoidant individuals are not always highly sexually active. In my practice, I met many people who have avoidant tendencies and are late bloomers who begin dating or becoming sexually active later than their peers. Others go through long periods of abstinence or have surprisingly limited relationship histories. One-night stands, casual encounters, and transactional forms of sex may feel safer because they provide physical closeness without the expectations, obligations, or emotional risks that often accompany committed relationships.

7. The Relationship Feels Physically Close But Emotionally Lonely

Perhaps the most painful sign is the feeling that someone is there but not really there. You may have a satisfying sex life but still experience loneliness when emotional connection never seems to deepen beyond a certain point.

Many avoidant individuals learned early in life that emotional needs were unwelcome, burdensome, or unsafe. As adults, they often develop impressive self-sufficiency and struggle to depend on others. In the bedroom, this can create a frustrating dynamic in which physical closeness is available, but genuine partnership remains just out of reach.

The Heartbreak of Loving an Avoidant Partner

Loving an avoidant partner can be heartbreaking. Beneath the distance, defensiveness, and emotional walls is often someone who learned long ago that closeness was unsafe. Many long for love, connection, and companionship, yet struggle to fully accept these things.

It can be painful to watch someone push away affection, support, and intimacy when it's exactly what they need. Partners often find themselves caught between empathy for their partner's wounds and fury over the ways those wounds continue to interfere with the relationship.

However, compassion should not come at the expense of your own needs. Understanding where these patterns come from does not mean accepting chronic emotional unavailability. Healthy relationships require effort from both people.

Avoidant attachment is not a life sentence. With self-awareness, willingness, and consistent self-work, people can learn to tolerate closeness, communicate more openly, and build secure connections. Offering patience and space is important, but only when it is accompanied by a genuine effort to move toward greater intimacy. Love alone cannot dismantle years of self-protection; the person behind those defenses must be willing to do that work as well.

item.title: Genes and Size, You Can’t Turn a Labrador Into a Greyhound
item.description:
Genetics

Genes and Size, You Can’t Turn a Labrador Into a Greyhound

Body shape and size are largely genetically determined.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Recovery from eating disorders includes accepting that body shape and size are largely genetically determined.
  • Eating disorder recovery requires adequate nutrition to repair the physical damage caused by malnutrition.
  • Health comes from supporting the body’s natural balance, not chasing unrealistic thinness ideals.
  • Peak athletic performance comes from a body that is properly nourished and functioning.

Kristin assumed her therapist would naturally understand that being thin was something to strive for and inherently desirable. She was surprised to learn that her therapist’s primary concern was not how her body looked, but how healthy it was. Her therapist explained that having a smaller-than-average or model-thin body is only healthy if it aligns with your natural genetics.

Source: Roberto Hund / Pexels

Body shape and size are largely determined by genetics. Although diet and exercise can influence body weight and shape to some degree, many people continue to believe that body size is entirely within personal control. As a result, the widespread assumption persists that proper diet and exercise should enable anyone to achieve an ideal body shape.

A useful analogy is asking a Labrador Retriever to achieve the body shape of a Greyhound, even though each breed is genetically programmed for a distinctly different body structure.

Kristen had achieved a model-thin appearance through severe food restriction and excessive exercise. Although this led to compliments and positive feedback about how she looked, her body was far from healthy. Her menstrual cycle had become scant or irregular, and body composition analysis revealed significant muscle loss along with an increased percentage of body fat. In response to ongoing malnutrition, her body had shifted into survival mode—breaking down muscle tissue to obtain essential protein and energy while conserving fat stores as a protective mechanism.

Kristen argued that people diet to lose weight all the time; she questioned why it should be considered problematic when she did the same. As an athlete, she believed that being lean and thin was essential to performing at her highest level—or so she had convinced herself. Yet she was forced to acknowledge that ongoing muscle loss was unlikely to improve athletic performance.

What disappointed Kristen most was learning that she would likely be unable to maintain her current weight and body size while also restoring her health. More than anything, she wished there were a way to regain lost muscle mass, restore normal menstruation, and normalize her metabolism without having to increase her nutritional intake to healthy levels and risk the body changes she feared.

Kristin found the motivation to restore her health only after coming to terms with her genetically determined body type and letting go of the belief that she needed to force her body to conform to an unrealistic standard of thinness. Recovery required restoring adequate nutrition—not only to repair the physical damage caused by malnutrition, but also to allow her body to return to the healthy state it was genetically designed to maintain. Ultimately, she had to discover for herself that peak athletic performance is achieved through a body functioning at optimal health, not by pursuing an idealized image of what she believed the “perfect athlete” should look like.
